newsitem.title: USA: U.S. panel urges new approach to protecting health.
newsitem.headline: U.S. panel urges new approach to protecting health.

text.p: Congress should take a comprehensive look at the environment when drafting anti-pollution laws instead of focusing on individual risks, a federal commission recommended in a report to be released Wednesday.

The current approach to writing laws for clean air, water, and land addresses each hazard one at a time, often failing to recognize that problems might be interrelated, according to the panel, which was appointed by Congress, President Clinton and the National Academy of Sciences.

"It doesn't answer questions about how you really make a difference in people's health and the health of the environment," said Gilbert Omenn, dean of the University of Washington's School of Public Health and Medicine, who headed the commission.

Salmon populations in the Pacific Northwest, for instance, have dwindled because of overfishing, irrigation, hydropower dams, timber harvesting, urban pollution and possibly radiation from nuclear reactors.
Omenn said Congressional committees, regulatory agencies, and environmental groups were too compartmentalized for each to see the big picture on health risks and pollution.

The report called for policymakers to look at contaminants in air, water and land all together, and trace their sources and exposure levels to reach more sound conclusions on what risks and what pollution sources should be addressed.

Omenn predicted that if the government applied the panel's approach it would find that its recent focus on so-called hazardous air pollutants, a category of cancer-causing chemicals, had been misguided.
Instead, he said, more attention should be paid to another category of pollutants, which includes smog, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxide and sulfur oxides.
